opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a bit of a provocative way to put it, but let me try to say what I mean. Text is, in a sense, the residue of science. It's the compressed output, the conclusions people reached after a long process that is mostly invisible on the page. When you read a paper, you see the clean argument, the final figure, the theorem. You don't see the hundred wrong ideas, the experiments that failed, the moment someone noticed that a curve didn't look the way it was supposed to. And that process is really where creativity lives.

A model trained on everything ever written learns the statistical structure of that residue extremely well. And from my own work on how deep networks learn hierarchical, compositional data, I'd say they are remarkably good at discovering the latent rules that generate the data. They can recombine pieces at different levels of abstraction. That's not trivial; it's a form of generalization that goes well beyond memorization. But recombining existing concepts within the grammar of what has been said is different from discovering that the grammar itself is wrong.

Many of the important steps in physics came from exactly that: realizing that the existing description was inconsistent with some observation, and inventing a new variable or a new way of looking at the problem. Think about the introduction of the renormalization group, or of entropy. Those weren't interpolations within the space of existing texts. They required contact with the world, with experiments, and with a kind of dissatisfaction, a sense that something doesn't fit.

So I'd say there are a few missing ingredients. One is interaction: the ability to act, to test, to get surprised by reality rather than by the next token. Another is something like a value system for what counts as a good question, which is very hard to extract from text because the text mostly records answers. And a third is the ability to build new representations that are not already implicitly present in the training distribution.

None of that means it's impossible in principle for machines. But I don't think simply scaling up text alone gets you there. You need the loop with the world.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says scientific creativity requires interaction with the world, including acting, testing, and encountering reality.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key point is that text is a very impoverished representation of how knowledge is actually produced. When you read a paper, or even a textbook, what you see is the polished end product. You don't see the ten failed attempts, the wrong intuitions, the moment where someone realized that two things they thought were unrelated were in fact the same thing. All of that is erased. So if you train only on what was written, you're learning the outputs of a process without ever observing the process itself.

And in physics, at least, that process is largely about interacting with the world. You have a model, it makes a prediction, nature tells you that you're wrong, and you're forced to revise. That feedback loop is where new concepts come from. Creativity, in the scientific sense, is not recombination of existing sentences, it is the construction of a new representation that compresses phenomena nobody had compressed before. Everything ever written, almost by definition, does not contain the representations that have not been invented yet.

There is also a more technical point that I find interesting. We know from studying how these models learn that they are extremely good at capturing the statistical structure of the data, the hierarchies, the correlations, the compositional rules. But the data you have is the data generated by past human minds, with their particular biases and blind spots. If you fit that distribution very well, you become a very good imitator of human reasoning as it has existed. To go beyond it, you need a source of novelty that is not in the training set, and historically that source has been experiment, or at least the ability to test ideas against something that is not itself text.

So I'm not saying it's impossible for a machine to be creative. I'm saying that reading, alone, is probably not the mechanism. You need something that plays the role of the laboratory, where the system can be surprised.

astra-6.text:
Because what is written is already the result of a very strong selection. In science, you have an idea, you try something, it fails, you change your mind. And at the end you write a paper that presents a fairly clean argument. Much of the process that allowed you to arrive there is absent from the text.

So learning from everything ever written could give you an extraordinary command of what we know, and perhaps suggest very interesting connections. But scientific creativity also involves deciding what to investigate when you don’t know the answer. Which experiment would distinguish two explanations? Which simplification preserves the essential physics? You need to confront your ideas with something that can tell you they are wrong.

I don’t think this is an argument that machines cannot be creative. It’s an argument that learning from text alone is missing an important part of the loop: proposing something, testing it, and learning from the discrepancy between what you expected and what happened.

r003.rationale: It says scientific creativity requires proposing ideas, testing them against what happens, and learning from the discrepancy—communicating interaction with the world.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think there is a difference between learning what people have written and learning how to ask nature a question. Scientific knowledge is not just a collection of statements. It comes from a process in which you have an idea, you work out what it predicts, and you confront that prediction with an experiment. Very often, what matters is precisely the discrepancy between what you expected and what you observe.

A machine trained on everything ever written could certainly identify connections that we have missed. I don’t see a fundamental reason why it couldn’t propose interesting theories. But that alone does not tell you whether those theories describe the world. For that, you need a feedback loop with reality: choosing what to measure, doing the experiment, and changing your picture when it fails.

And in science, finding the right question can be harder than answering it. You have to decide which details are essential, which you can ignore, and what simple description might explain the phenomenon. Learning the existing literature is a powerful starting point, but it isn’t the whole activity.
